### Problem: Product of Array Except Self {#sec-pref-p5-a}

::: {.p-statement}
Given $a$ ($2 \le n \le 10^5$, $-30 \le a_i \le 30$), return an array `out` with `out[i]` equal to the product of all elements of $a$ **except** $a[i]$. You may not use division, and the intended solution is $O(n)$ time without counting on extra space beyond the output.

Source: [LC 238 · Product of Array Except Self](https://leetcode.com/problems/product-of-array-except-self/){.solved difficulty="Medium"}
:::

::: {.p-intuition}
"Everything except me" is "everything to my left times everything to my right". Left products and right products are prefix and suffix tables of the same operation — and because a zero destroys division, the no-inverse shape from @sec-pref-other is not just cleaner, it is the only correct answer.
:::

::: {.p-approach}
1. **Brute force.** For each $i$, multiply all $j \ne i$: $O(n^2)$.
2. **Two tables.** Build `L` forward and `R` backward, then `out[i] = L[i]*R[i]`: $O(n)$ time, $O(n)$ extra space.
3. **Fold one table into the output.** Use `out` itself to hold `L` during the forward pass, then walk backwards carrying a single running product `run`. Same time, $O(1)$ auxiliary space (@sec-arr-inplace).

**Invariant.** After the forward pass `out[i]` $= \prod_{k<i} a[k]$; during the backward pass `run` $= \prod_{k>i} a[k]$, so the moment they are multiplied `out[i]` is final and never revisited.
:::

The buttons are in order. Each one keeps the previous solution and changes only what that form changes.

::: {.panel-tabset .solution-forms}

#### Multiply every other element

::: {.form-next}
Take "except self" literally: for each $i$, walk the whole array and multiply everything that is not $a[i]$. Always right, needs no table, and $O(n^2)$ — the same products are recomputed from scratch at every position.
:::

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}
##### Python

```{python}
def product_except_self_brute(a):
    from math import prod
    return [prod(a[k] for k in range(len(a)) if k != i) for i in range(len(a))]
```

##### C++

```cpp
#include <vector>
using namespace std;

vector<int> productExceptSelfBrute(vector<int>& nums) {
    int n = (int)nums.size();
    vector<int> out(n);
    for (int i = 0; i < n; ++i) {
        long long p = 1;
        for (int k = 0; k < n; ++k) if (k != i) p *= nums[k];
        out[i] = (int)p;
    }
    return out;
}
```
:::

#### A left table and a right table

::: {.form-next}
"Everything except me" is "everything to my left times everything to my right", and those are a prefix and a suffix table of the same product. Build `L` forward and `R` backward, then `out[i] = L[i] * R[i]`: $O(n)$ time, $O(n)$ extra space, and no division — so a zero anywhere cannot break it (@sec-pref-other).
:::

```{python}

#| renderings: [light, dark]
def draw(ax, p):
    title, inp, steps, final = Traces.get("prod", "tables")
    assert str(final) == "[24, 12, 8, 6]"
    V.story(ax, p, title, inp, steps, final)
V.show(draw)
```

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}
##### Python

```{python}
def product_except_self_tables(a):
    n = len(a)
    L = [1] * n
    for i in range(1, n):
        L[i] = L[i - 1] * a[i - 1]          # product strictly left of i
    R = [1] * n
    for i in range(n - 2, -1, -1):
        R[i] = R[i + 1] * a[i + 1]          # product strictly right of i
    return [L[i] * R[i] for i in range(n)]
```

##### C++

```cpp
#include <vector>
using namespace std;

vector<int> productExceptSelfTables(vector<int>& nums) {
    int n = (int)nums.size();
    vector<long long> L(n, 1), R(n, 1);
    for (int i = 1; i < n; ++i) L[i] = L[i - 1] * nums[i - 1];
    for (int i = n - 2; i >= 0; --i) R[i] = R[i + 1] * nums[i + 1];
    vector<int> out(n);
    for (int i = 0; i < n; ++i) out[i] = (int)(L[i] * R[i]);
    return out;
}
```
:::

#### Fold the right table into one variable

::: {.form-next}
Only one right-product is ever live as you sweep backwards, so the `R` table is space you can hand back. Reuse `out` to hold `L` after the forward pass, then carry the right products in a single `run` and multiply in place. Same time, $O(1)$ auxiliary — the in-place trick of @sec-arr-inplace.
:::

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| renderings: [light, dark]
def draw(ax, p):
    title, inp, steps, final = Traces.get("prod", "one")
    assert str(final) == "[24, 12, 8, 6]"
    V.story(ax, p, title, inp, steps, final)
V.show(draw)
```

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}
##### Python

```{python}
#| label: arr-product-except-self
def product_except_self(a: list[int]) -> list[int]:
    n = len(a)
    out = [1] * n
    for i in range(1, n):
        out[i] = out[i - 1] * a[i - 1]      # forward pass: left products
    run = 1
    for i in range(n - 2, -1, -1):
        run *= a[i + 1]                     # right products, one variable
        out[i] *= run
    return out


for _ in range(300):
    a = [random.randint(-4, 4) for _ in range(random.randint(2, 9))]
    assert product_except_self(a) == product_except_self_brute(a) == product_except_self_tables(a)

assert product_except_self([1, 2, 3, 4]) == [24, 12, 8, 6]    # the board sample
assert product_except_self([-1, 1, 0, -3, 3]) == [0, 0, 9, 0, 0]
assert product_except_self([0, 0]) == [0, 0]
assert product_except_self([2, 3]) == [3, 2]
print("product_except_self OK")
```

##### C++

```cpp
#include <vector>
using namespace std;

vector<int> productExceptSelf(vector<int>& nums) {
    int n = (int)nums.size();
    vector<int> out(n, 1);
    for (int i = 1; i < n; ++i)                       // left products
        out[i] = (int)((long long)out[i - 1] * nums[i - 1]);
    long long run = 1;                                // right products
    for (int i = n - 2; i >= 0; --i) {
        run *= nums[i + 1];
        out[i] = (int)((long long)out[i] * run);
    }
    return out;
}
```
:::
:::

::: {.p-complexity}
**Multiply every other element** is $O(n^2)$ time, $O(1)$ extra. **A left table and a right table** is $O(n)$ time and $O(n)$ space: two full passes to build `L` and `R`, one to combine. **Fold the right table into one variable** keeps the $O(n)$ time but drops to $O(1)$ auxiliary — the output array holds `L`, and `run` holds the live right product, so no second table exists. Magnitudes: with $|a_i| \le 30$ and $n$ up to $10^5$ an arbitrary product would overflow any fixed-width type, so LeetCode adds the guarantee that every prefix and suffix product fits in a 32-bit integer; the code still does each multiply in 64-bit before narrowing, the habit @sec-arr-cost teaches.
:::

::: {.p-edge}
- One zero in the array: every `out[i]` is $0$ except the zero's own cell. A divide-based "total / a[i]" must special-case it: the total is $0$, so the zero's own cell would divide by zero, yet its true answer is the (usually non-zero) product of the others. The two-pass version needs no case analysis (@sec-pref-other).
- Two or more zeros: all answers are $0$ — still no special case.
- Negative values: products flip sign, and `run` handles it because multiplication is associative over the whole range.
- $n = 2$: each answer is the other element; both passes run exactly once.
:::
